I, anything were wanted to show the utter unfitnees of the preemie system of allowing county affairs to be managed by • nominated body of magietrates, the want was supplied by the nroceedings of the Cheshire Quarter eatsioni at lin uteford on Monday It hap- pened that the govertiorship of the Howe of Correction was vacant by the death of that tad and valued servant of the county—Mr. Oallop—and • few weeks ago it was agreed ' that a committee should look through the testimonials of all the candidates, select the five beet men and present them to the court. Of course it was Impapible to include the right of nominating any other candidate at the time of election, and on Monday two magistrates proposed and seconded a sixth candidate, who was included therefore among those to be voted for, and who re• ceived 27 votes, all, we believe, without ex- ception, from magistrates living within a few miles of the candidate, and not one for anyone who lived outside the influence of acquaintance and neighbourhood, or who had the smallest idea that merit and not friendship ought to be the reason for an ap- pointment to a public office. Now, in the Mat place, we have to say that those gentlemen who proposed the candidate were in duty bound, instead of merely making a formal nomination,. to have alleged some reason why the Cial• mittee had passed over the claims of their favourite unfairly. Fraud, favouritism, prejudice, a disposition to post- pone one clasp to another, a hurried examin- ation of testimonials might all have been urged as reasons why the decision of the Committee should be questioned. But no thing of the sort was done. These gentle- men played the game simply, neither a very noble nor a very courteous one, "of heads win, tails you lose." They were content to glow the Committee to be appointed, and if their candidate had been chosen, to have used the opinions f the Committee am an argument in his favour, but as he was not chosen they then were not ashamed to ignore the trouble and time which had been spent, and to bring forward without one wordofri commendation or apology a man for whom they had nothing to say, and whose virtues , were oomprieed in a respectable career in the army, a short connection with the manufacture of soda-water, and such an acquaintance with the governor of one of our prisons as to have enabled him to see the working of the inside of it. And this man wee put in competition with men whose life had been devoted to prison work and prison organization, with men who had had the management oh training ships, who had had for years practical experience of the govern- ment t.f bodies of men, and the responsi- bility of the chergee of ships and prisons. As this miserable attempt at parochialism has failed, we should not have felt it to be our duty to allude to it but for two reasons. The first one is, that it shows how utterly irresponsible a man becomes as soon as he is appointed a member of a g earning body for life, and has no occasion to seek re- election. Can anyone believe that with the fear of Constituencies before their eyes, these 27 gentlemen would have dared to vote for a candidate in whose favour they had nothing special to urge, and whose testimonials were, to say the feast, so obviously inferior to those of the live selected? But they were safe in their honours, and it mattered lit le to them whether the beet man was elected or not, if they could do a good turn to a niend. We do them the justice to believe that Ijyv would not have voted for an abso- lutely uiffit man, but surely when candidates are invited to send in their tootle:loniae there is an implied understanding that the best man should be elected, and it is unfair and dishonourable to postpone superior claims of experience and merit to a feeling of private friendship. And this brings us to our second point, that the average Englishman has unfortu- nately got it into his head that all elections are for the benefit of the elected, and not for that of the electors. In the case before us, we believe that the gentleman on whom the vote of the magietracy at last fell, conferred a greater favour on them in applying for the post than they did on him by giving it to him. It is this false and wretched notion that causes canvassing, that leads to bribing and treating, that de. grades the candidates and vitiates the elec- tors. Of course where there is a salary attaehed to an office it may be said that a candidate has objects to gain, and that he receives as well as gives a boon, though in many cases the salary is ridiculously inade- quate to the work, and the real reason of the application is the. hatred which men have to idleness, but in cases where there a nothing but I work and honour, surely the electors should remember that they are, after all, the obliged party, that their chief desire sh .uld be to choose the best man, and that the best man does them a honour in consenting to be chosen. This is a lesson which all our Con- stituencies, Parliamentary. Municipal, Local Board, have to learn, and until they have learned it, we shall not get thoroughly rid of the corrupting influence of a personal can- vass, and votes given to those who ask the oftenest, and who too frequently accompany ' their request with something even mere seductive than the human voice, and more acceptable than a mere prayer.
